rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the Prophet forgot nothing after this verse descended.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي : إنه عليه السلام لم ينس بعد نزول هذه الآية شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the nonliteral-exception reading, the phrase may teach blessing by saying “if God wills,” as God does even while knowing all outcomes.
rows.anchor: فأنت وأمتك يا محمد أولى بها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says God did not will the Prophet to forget; the exception only declares that God could make him forget if He chose.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : إنه تعالى ما شاء أن ينسى محمد عليه السلام شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This hypothetical exception teaches that the Prophet’s not forgetting is God’s grace and kindness, not his own power.
rows.anchor: فائدة هذا الاستثناء أن الله تعالى يعرفه قدرة ربه حتى يعلم أن عدم النسيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning the exception kept the Prophet alert and careful with every revelation, since any amount might have been excepted.
rows.anchor: جوز رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في كل ما ينزل عليه من الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception may simply negate forgetting altogether, as in an idiom that adds an exception without intending to exclude anything.
rows.anchor: أن يكون الغرض من قوله : { إلا ما شاء الله } نفي النسيان رأسا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj reads a real exception: the Prophet might temporarily forget and then remember, without permanent total forgetting.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : إلا ما شاء الله أن ينسى ، فإنه ينسى ثم يتذكر بعد ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet omitted a verse while praying; Ubay thought it had been abrogated, but the Prophet said he had forgotten it.
rows.anchor: فحسب أبي أنها نسخت ، فسأله فقال : نسيتها

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil interprets forgetting as abrogation: God may withdraw a verse and command that it no longer be recited or prayed with.
rows.anchor: فيأمرك أن لا تقرأه ولا تصلي به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A real exception could mean rare minor lapses, but not forgetting religious obligations, which would damage the law and is impermissible.
rows.anchor: ويشترط أن لا يكون ذلك القليل من واجبات الشرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He knows what is public and hidden” may mean God knows the Prophet’s audible recitation with Gabriel and his private fear, and will relieve it.
rows.anchor: وعالم بالسر الذي في قلبك وهو أنك تخاف النسيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the Prophet forgets only what God wills to abrogate, since God knows where abrogation serves people’s interests.
rows.anchor: أن ينسخ ، فإنه أعلم بمصالح العبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zarābī are carpets or rugs; zarbiyya and zarbī are singular forms, with zāy kasra according to all linguists; mabthūtha means spread out or scattered among gathering places.
rows.anchor: يعني البسط والطنافس واحدها زربية وزربي بكسر الزاي في قول جميع أهل اللغة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The word musayṭir means one who dominates or has power over them.
rows.anchor: { بمسيطر } بمسلط ، كقوله : { يقولون وما أنت عليهم بجبار }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was commanded only to remind; he was not appointed to kill people or coerce them into faith.
rows.anchor: المعنى أنك ما أمرت إلا بالتذكير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Tamim speech the ṭāʾ may be fatḥa because sayṭara is transitive there.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو في لغة تميم مفتوح الطاء على أن سيطر متعد عندهم

rows.speaker: جميع المفسرين
rows.claim: The commentators say the command not to dominate was abrogated by the fighting verse.
rows.anchor: ثم نسختها آية القتال ، هذا قول جميع المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the word was already discussed under “Or are they the controllers?”
rows.anchor: قد تقدم عند قوله : { أم هم المسيطرون }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that God will account for them continues the threat of the greater punishment and consoles the Prophet: their return is to the appointed reckoning.
rows.anchor: ليزيل به عن قلب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم حزنه على كفرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although exacting punishment is God’s right, He must exact it either because His promise cannot fail or because wisdom requires redress for the oppressed.
rows.anchor: إما في الحكمة ، فإنه لو لم ينتقم للمظلوم من الظالم

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر المدني
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani reads ayyābahum with a doubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر المدني : { إيابهم } بالتشديد

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The doubled form may derive from ayyāb as a fīʿāl verbal noun, or from awāb changed through īwāb, by analogy with dīwān from dūwān.
rows.anchor: وجهه أن يكون فيعالا مصدره أيب فيعل من الإياب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting the return phrase first intensifies the warning: they return only to the Omnipotent, and only He accounts for even the tiniest thing.
rows.anchor: فائدة تقديم الظرف التشديد بالوعيد ، فإن { إيابهم } ليس إلا إلى الجبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nights are indefinite because they possess special virtues unavailable at other times; indefiniteness signals immense merit.
rows.anchor: لأنها ليال مخصوصة بفضائل لا تحصل في غيرها والتنكير دال على الفضيلة العظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view identifies the nights as the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, when pilgrimage rites are performed; a report says righteous deeds then are especially meritorious.
rows.anchor: أنها عشر ذي الحجة لأنها أيام الاشتغال بهذا النسك في الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies them as the ten days of Muharram, including ʿĀshūrāʾ, whose fasting has reported merit.
rows.anchor: وفيها يوم عاشوراء ولصومه من الفضل ما ورد به الأخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view identifies them as the last ten nights of Ramadan because they include Laylat al-Qadr; a report urges seeking it then.
rows.anchor: وفيها ليلة القدر ، إذ في الخبر «اطلبوها في العشر الأخير من رمضان »

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet, when the last ten nights of Ramadan began, tightened his waist, refrained from sex, and woke his family for night prayer.
rows.anchor: وأيقظ أهله أي كف عن الجماع وأمر أهله بالتهجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shafʿ and watr mean even and odd, called khasā and zakā by Arabs; the common terms are pair and individual.
rows.anchor: هو الذي تسميه العرب الخسا والزكا والعامة الزوج والفرد

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports that people of ʿĀliya pronounce watr with fatḥa for a number and kasra for blood feud, while Tamim uses kasra for both.
rows.anchor: قال يونس : أهل العالية يقولون الوتر بالفتح في العدد والوتر بالكسر في الذحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb awtara means to make something odd; the Prophet’s instruction to use an odd number when cleaning with stones supplies an example.
rows.anchor: وتقول أوترته أوتره إيتارا أي جعلته وترا

rows.speaker: الحسن والأعمش وابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn ʿAbbās read watr with kasra.
rows.anchor: والكسر قراءة الحسن والأعمش وابن عباس

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة
rows.claim: The people of Medina read watr with fatḥa, the Hijazi dialect form.
rows.anchor: والفتح قراءة أهل المدينة وهي لغة حجازية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the closest interpretation is the Day of Sacrifice as shafʿ and the Day of ʿArafa as watr, since both days have exceptional pilgrimage merits.
rows.anchor: أن الشفع يوم النحر والوتر يوم عرفة ، وإنما أقسم الله بهما لشرفهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of ʿArafa is central to pilgrimage, as the hadith says, “Pilgrimage is ʿArafa”; sacrifice and major rites occur on the Day of Sacrifice.
rows.anchor: كما في الحديث ( الحج عرفة ) وأما يوم النحر فيقع فيه القربان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report calls the Day of Sacrifice the greater pilgrimage day.
rows.anchor: فلما اختص هذان اليومان بهذه الفضائل لا جرم أقسم الله بهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes shafʿ the first two and watr the third of the post-sacrifice Days of Tashrīq, encompassing the remaining pilgrimage rites.
rows.anchor: الشفع هو يومان بعد يوم النحر ، الوتر هو اليوم الثالث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supporters of the Tashrīq view say it avoids reusing the two days already included among the ten and includes the days on which some rites occur.
rows.anchor: أن العيد وعرفة دخلا في العشر ، فوجب أن يكون المراد بالشفع والوتر غيرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A view calls Adam watr and his wife shafʿ; another calls Adam and Eve shafʿ and God watr.
rows.anchor: الوتر آدم شفع بزوجته ، وفي رواية أخرى الشفع آدم وحواء والوتر هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view interprets watr as the odd-numbered prayers, such as Maghrib, and shafʿ as even-numbered prayers; a report from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn attributes this to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: روى عمران بن الحصين عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : ( هي الصلوات منها شفع ومنها وتر )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes all creation shafʿ, citing that God created everything in pairs, and God Himself watr.
rows.anchor: لقوله تعالى : { ومن كل شيء خلقنا زوجين } وقوله : { وخلقناكم أزواجا }

rows.speaker: بعض المتكلمين
rows.claim: Some theologians reject identifying God as watr: the oath means “Lord of the even and odd,” so watr should be a created thing; God is not paired this way, and the relevant report is not firmly established.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المتكلمين : لا يصح أن يقال الوتر هو الله لوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes shafʿ and watr to include every creature, since no created thing is outside being paired or odd; it compares the oath to one by all visible and invisible things.
rows.anchor: أن شيئا من المخلوقات لا ينفك عن كونه شفعا ووترا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes shafʿ the eight levels of Paradise and watr the seven levels of Hell.
rows.anchor: الشفع درجات الجنة وهي ثمانية ، والوتر دركات النار وهي سبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes shafʿ paired human attributes and watr the divine attributes, which are without opposites or deficiency.
rows.anchor: الشفع صفات الخلق كالعلم والجهل والقدرة والعجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view understands the terms as even and odd number themselves; number enables calculation of worship times, days, and months.
rows.anchor: المراد بالشفع والوتر ، نفس العدد فكأنه أقسم بالحساب

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says shafʿ is days and nights, while watr is Resurrection Day, after which no night follows.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل الشفع هو الأيام والليالي والوتر هو اليوم الذي لا ليل بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation calls prophets with two names shafʿ, such as Muḥammad and Aḥmad, and prophets with one name watr.
rows.anchor: الشفع كل نبي له اسمان مثل محمد وأحمد والمسيح وعيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes Adam and Eve shafʿ and Mary watr.
rows.anchor: الشفع آدم وحواء والوتر مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the twelve springs given to Moses shafʿ and his nine signs watr.
rows.anchor: والوتر الآيات التسع التي أوتي موسى في قوله : { ولقد آتينا موسى تسع آيات بينات }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation calls the days of ʿĀd shafʿ and their nights watr.
rows.anchor: الشفع أيام عاد والوتر لياليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the twelve zodiacal mansions shafʿ and the seven planets watr.
rows.anchor: الشفع البروج الاثنا عشر لقوله تعالى : { جعل في السماء بروجا } والوتر الكواكب السبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation calls a thirty-day month shafʿ and a twenty-nine-day month watr.
rows.anchor: الشفع الشهر الذي يتم ثلاثين يوما ، والوتر الشهر الذي يتم تسعة وعشرين يوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the limbs shafʿ and the heart watr, since a person has only one heart.
rows.anchor: الشفع الأعضاء والوتر القلب ، قال تعالى : { ما جعل الله لرجل من قلبين في جوفه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the two lips shafʿ and the tongue watr.
rows.anchor: الشفع الشفتان والوتر اللسان قال تعالى : { ولسانا وشفتين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the two prostrations shafʿ and the single bowing watr.
rows.anchor: الشفع السجدتان والوتر الركوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the eight gates of Paradise shafʿ and the seven gates of Hell watr.
rows.anchor: الشفع أبواب الجنة لأنها ثمانية والوتر أبواب النار لأنها سبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All these interpretations are possible, but the wording does not specify one; absent a Prophetic report or consensus, they should be stated as possibilities, and the definite article may indicate the whole class.
rows.anchor: والظاهر لا إشعار له بشيء من هذه الأشياء على التعيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Iram names the tribe, it explains ʿĀd and signals the ancient first ʿĀd; if it names a town, “people of Iram” is understood with an omitted genitive.
rows.anchor: جعلناه اسم القبيلة كان قوله : { إرم } عطف بيان لعاد

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr’s genitive reading, “ʿĀd of Iram,” supports taking Iram as a town.
rows.anchor: ويدل عليه قراءة ابن الزبير بعاد إرم على الإضافة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads ʿĀd and Iram both with fatḥa.
rows.anchor: قرأ الحسن : { بعاد إرم } مفتوحين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading leaves rāʾ in Iram unvowelled for ease, like the reading of warqikum.
rows.anchor: وقرئ : { بعاد إرم } بسكون الراء على التخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading attaches Iram to “possessor of pillars”; a further reading makes the phrase an apposition to “what your Lord did,” meaning He made it ruined.
rows.anchor: وقرئ : { بعاد إرم ذات العماد } بإضافة { إرم } إلى { ذات العماد }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Iram is the tribe, “possessor of pillars” may describe their tent poles, their tall column-like bodies, or their lofty construction.
rows.anchor: كانوا بدويين يسكنون الأخبية والخيام والخباء لابد فيها من العماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Iram is a city, it means a place of columns and high buildings; ʿĀd built raised structures and palaces on pillars.
rows.anchor: إن جعلناه اسم البلد فالمعنى أنها ذات أساطين أي ذات أبنية مرفوعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says Shaddād and Shadīd, sons of ʿĀd, ruled and subdued others; after Shadīd died, Shaddād ruled the world and built a golden, jeweled paradise-city over three hundred years.
rows.anchor: روي أنه كان لعاد ابنان شداد وشديد فملكا وقهرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Shaddād approached his city with his people, a heavenly cry destroyed them a day’s journey away; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qulāba later found it while searching for camels and took what he could.
rows.anchor: فلما كان منها على مسيرة يوم وليلة بعث الله عليهم صيحة من السماء فهلكوا

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb identified Ibn Qulāba’s discovery as Iram and predicted a short, fair Muslim with two moles would enter it while searching for camels; he identified Ibn Qulāba as that man.
rows.anchor: فقال : هي إرم ذات العماد ، وسيدخلها رجل من المسلمين في زمانك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes “its like” to mean ʿĀd’s own bodily size and strength; each man was 400 cubits tall and could kill a crowd by hurling a huge rock.
rows.anchor: أي مثل عاد في البلاد في عظم الجثة وشدة القوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading compares Iram with every city in the world; Ibn al-Zubayr reads the phrase with God explicitly as its subject.
rows.anchor: لم يخلق مثل مدينة شداد في جميع بلاد الدنيا ، وقرأ ابن الزبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading refers “its like” to the pillars, construing al-ʿimād as the plural of ʿamud.
rows.anchor: أن الكناية عائدة إلى العماد أي لم يخلق مثل تلك الأساطين في البلاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account warns disbelievers: God destroyed ʿĀd for disbelief and rejecting messengers despite their exceptional advantages, so weaker unbelievers have greater reason to fear.
rows.anchor: فإنه تعالى بين أنه أهلكهم بما كفروا وكذبوا الرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says Pharaoh was called “possessor of stakes” because of his many soldiers and their tents pitched when they camped.
rows.anchor: أنه سمي ذا الأوتاد لكثرة جنوده ومضاربهم التي كانوا يضربونها إذا نزلوا

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports Pharaoh impaled his wife with four stakes, put a millstone on her chest, and exposed her to the sun; she prayed for a house in Paradise, which God unveiled for her to see.
rows.anchor: روى عن أبي هريرة أن فرعون وتد لامرأته أربعة أوتاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes stakes figuratively as the foundations of kingship and men, supported by a poetic line using the image of firm stakes.
rows.anchor: كما قال الشاعر : في ظل ملك راسخ الأوتاد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the stakes were play structures under which people played for Pharaoh; the report passes through Qatāda and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: روى قتادة عن سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس : أن تلك الأوتاد كانت ملاعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “those who transgressed” may refer only to Pharaoh, its nearest antecedent, but al-Razi prefers that it include everyone previously mentioned.
rows.anchor: يرجع إلى جميع من تقدم ذكرهم ، وهذا هو الأقرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best parsing puts “those who transgressed” in the accusative as censure; nominative predication or genitive description of ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh are also possible.
rows.anchor: أحسن الوجوه في إعرابه أن يكون في محل النصب على الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their transgression means committing sins and tyrannizing over God’s prophets and believers.
rows.anchor: عملوا المعاصي وتجبروا على أنبياء الله والمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Corruption is the opposite of righteousness: as righteousness includes every kind of good, corruption includes every kind of sin; whoever disobeys God or rules unjustly is corrupt.
rows.anchor: فكما أن الصلاح يتناول جميع أقسام البر ، فالفساد يتناول جميع أقسام الإثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression “poured the lash of punishment” is an idiom for striking or covering someone with blows; the lash signals that worldly punishment is small beside the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: وذكر السوط إشارة إلى أن ما أحله بهم في الدنيا من العذاب العظيم

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī compares the image to lashes repeatedly poured onto a victim until they kill him.
rows.anchor: وشبهه بصب السوط الذي يتواتر على المضروب فيهلكه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan said God has many lashes and seized them with one of them.
rows.anchor: إذا قرأ هذه الآية قال : إن عند الله أسواطا كثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although another verse says God would leave no creature on earth if He seized people for their deeds, the complete recompense is deferred to the Hereafter; worldly punishment is a foretaste.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تقتضي تأخير تمام الجزاء إلى الآخرة والواقع في الدنيا شيء من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mirṣād is a place where a watcher waits, on the pattern mifʿāl from raṣada as mīqāt is from waqata; it pictures God awaiting sinners’ punishment so they cannot escape.
rows.anchor: المرصاد المكان الذي يترقب فيه الراصد مفعال من رصده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An Arab, asked where God is, answered that He is at the watchpost.
rows.anchor: وعن بعض العرب أنه قيل له : أين ربك ؟ فقال : بالمرصاد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says God watches the deeds of humanity.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : يرصد أعمال بني آدم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains the phrase as “to Him is the return”; al-Razi says this and al-Hasan’s view apply to believers and unbelievers alike.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : إليه المصير ، وهذان الوجهان عامان للمؤمنين والكافرين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj restricts the threat to those who disbelieve in God and turn away from obedience, whom He watches for punishment.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : يرصد من كفر به وعدل عن طاعته بالعذاب

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says God awaits the unjust and disobedient for punishment; al-Razi calls the interpretations close.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك : يرصد لأهل الظلم والمعصية

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil glosses the phrase as failing to feed a poor person; its meaning is that they do not urge others to feed one.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : ولا تطعمون مسكينا ، والمعنى لا تأمرون بإطعامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with yāʾ, taḥāḍḍūn, means that people do not urge one another, with the first tāʾ of tatafāʿalūn elided.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ ولا تحاضون أراد تتحاضون فحذف تاء تتفاعلون

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd’s reading has the tāʾ vowelled with ḍamma and means mutual urging.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة ابن مسعود : { ولا تحاضون } بضم التاء من المحاضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turāth derives from wirāth, with tāʾ replacing initial wāw under the same pattern as tijāh from wijāh.
rows.anchor: أصل التراث وراث ، والتاء تبدل من الواو المضمومة نحو تجاه ووجاه

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says lamm means forceful gathering; it describes a compact troop or stone, and the eater gathers and consumes all food on a platter.
rows.anchor: قال الليث : اللم الجمع الشديد ، ومنه كتيبة ملمومة وحجر ملموم

rows.speaker: الواحدي والمفسرون
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī and commentators call “forceful eating” a paraphrase rather than a precise gloss; grammatically lamm is a verbal noun used adjectivally to mean an eater who gathers and consumes greedily.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي والمفسرون : يقولون في قوله : { أكلا لما } أي شديدا وهو حل معنى وليس بتفسير

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says they consumed orphans’ inheritance wastefully and hastily, gathering all of it together.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : كانوا يأكلون أموال اليتامى إسرافا وبدارا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says they ate both their own share and their companion’s share, joining another’s portion to theirs.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن : أي يأكلون نصيبهم ونصيب صاحبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says heirs gather and consume the entire estate, mixing what is lawful with what is doubtful and forbidden.
rows.anchor: فالوارث يلم الكل أي يضم البعض إلى البعض ويأخذ الكل ويأكله

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf says the blame may target heirs who acquire wealth easily, then lavish it on abundant delicacies and pleasures like idle heirs.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الذم متوجها إلى الوارث الذي ظفر بالمال سهلا مهلا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr says jamm yajumm means to increase, of wealth or other things; jamm means abundant.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو جم يجم أي يكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means an intense, abundant love of wealth, showing that people focus solely on worldly life and turn from the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: والمعنى : ويحبون المال حبا كثيرا شديدا ، فبين أن حرصهم على الدنيا فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rational proof establishes that motion is impossible for God: anything moving is a body, and bodies cannot be eternal, so the verse needs figurative interpretation.
rows.anchor: ثبت بالدليل العقلي أن الحركة على الله تعالى محال ، لأن كل ما كان كذلك كان جسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation supplies an omitted genitive: the command of God arrives to reckon and recompense.
rows.anchor: وجاء أمر ربك بالمحاسبة والمجازاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation supplies “power”: God’s overpowering comes, like saying that the Umayyads came to mean their power came.
rows.anchor: وجاء قهر ربك كما يقال جاءتنا بنو أمية أي قهرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says the great signs of God come into view on Resurrection Day, and their appearance is expressed as His own coming to glorify them.
rows.anchor: وجاء جلائل آيات ربك لأن هذا يكون يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation means God’s manifestation: knowledge of Him becomes immediate on that day as doubts and uncertainty disappear.
rows.anchor: وجاء ظهور ربك ، وذلك لأن معرفة الله تصير في ذلك اليوم ضرورية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording may also depict the display of God’s signs and sovereignty by analogy with a king whose personal arrival inspires more awe than his whole army.
rows.anchor: مثلت حاله في ذلك بحال الملك إذا حضر بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A final possibility takes rabb as “nurturer”: the greatest angel who nurtures the Prophet may be the referent.
rows.anchor: أن الرب هو المربى ، ولعل ملكا هو أعظم الملائكة هو مربي للنبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels descend from each heaven and stand row after row, surrounding jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: تنزل ملائكة كل سماء فيصطفون صفا بعد صف محدقين بالجن والإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view reads ḥill as “resident”: the Prophet dwells in this city.
rows.anchor: وأنت مقيم بهذا البلد نازل فيه

rows.speaker: شرحبيل
rows.claim: A second view reads ḥill as “lawful”: Meccans preserve the sanctuary’s prohibitions but regard the Prophet’s life as lawful to attack or expel, although they know his virtue.
rows.anchor: عن شرحبيل : يحرمون أن يقتلوا بها صيدا أو يعضوا بها شجرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This contrast reassures the Prophet and urges him to bear Meccan abuse, while expressing amazement at their hostility toward him.
rows.anchor: وفيه تثبيت لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وبعث على احتمال ما كان يكابد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda reads ḥill as permission for the Prophet to kill whom he wished in Mecca when God opened it for him, a unique permission; he killed Ibn Khaṭal at the Kaʿba and Miqyās ibn Ṣubāba, and secured Abū Sufyān’s house.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : { وأنت حل } أي لست بآثم ، وحلال لك أن تقتل بمكة من شئت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet said Mecca was forbidden by God from the creation of heaven and earth until the Hour, and was made lawful for him only for an hour by day; he specified sanctuary protections.
rows.anchor: فهي حرام إلى أن تقوم الساعة لم تحل لأحد قبلي

rows.speaker: العباس
rows.claim: Al-ʿAbbās requested an exception for idhkhir grass used in houses and graves, and the Prophet granted it.
rows.anchor: فقال العباس : إلا الإذخر يا رسول الله فإنه لبيوتنا وقبورنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the sūra is Meccan and says “you are lawful” in the present tense, it may refer to a certain future event, since the certain future is like the present to God.
rows.anchor: وهذا من الله أحسن ، لأن المستقبل عنده كالحاضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says the Prophet did not commit forbidden acts in the town, honoring the sanctuary, unlike the polytheists who committed disbelief and denied messengers there.
rows.anchor: وأنت غير مرتكب في هذا البلد ما يحرم عليك ارتكابه تعظيما منك لهذا البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God swears by this honored town, “you are ḥill here” may mean the Prophet belongs to it; its people know his noble origin and lifelong purity, establishing his rank.
rows.anchor: أي وأنت من حل هذه البلدة المعظمة المكرمة ، وأهل هذا البلد يعرفون أصلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “And a begetter and what he begot” is coordinated with the oath by the town; the address about the Prophet intervenes between the coordinated parts.
rows.anchor: هذا معطوف على قوله : { لا أقسم بهذا البلد } وقوله : { وأنت حل بهذا البلد } معترض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes the begetter as Adam and what he begot as his descendants; humanity is wondrous in speech, reason, knowledge, prophethood, and service to God, and God honored Adam and taught him names.
rows.anchor: الولد آدم وما ولد ذريته ، أقسم بهم إذ هم من أعجب خلق الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some restrict the descendants to Adam’s righteous offspring, treating wicked people as non-descendants or like cattle, as in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو قسم بآدم والصالحين من أولاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies Abraham as father and Ishmael and Muhammad as what he begot: Mecca is sworn by, Abraham built it, and the other two dwelt there; the indefinite form adds praise and wonder.
rows.anchor: الولد إبراهيم وإسماعيل وما ولد محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes Abraham as begetter and all his descendants as offspring, including Arabs and non-Arabs across Syria, Egypt, Jerusalem, Arabia, and the Romans descended from Esau.
rows.anchor: الولد إبراهيم وما ولد جميع ولد إبراهيم بحيث يحتمل العرب والعجم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some narrow Abraham’s offspring to Arabs, and others to Arab Muslims; al-Razi reasons for the believers from the prayer invoking blessings on Abraham and his family.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من خص ذلك بولد إبراهيم من العرب ومنهم من خص ذلك بالعرب المسلمين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the begetter is one who gives birth and “what does not give birth” is what is begotten; mā is negation, but the construction requires an implied relative pronoun that Basran grammarians reject.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن عباس أنه قال : الولد الذي يلد ، وما ولد الذي لا يلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view means every parent and child, fitting the oath because it includes the inviolable worth of all creatures.
rows.anchor: يعني كل والد ومولود ، وهذا مناسب ، لأن حرمة الخلق كلهم داخل في هذا الكلام

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda reads the verse as asking whether the person thinks God has not seen him or will not ask how he earned and spent his wealth.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : أيظن أن الله لم يره ولم يسأله عن ماله من أين اكتسبه

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the man lied and gave nothing; God saw whether he gave or withheld and knew that his claim was false.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي : كان كاذبا لم ينفق شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing the believers, God identifies their Judgment-Day status as the people of the right, as He described in Sūrat al-Wāqiʿa.
rows.anchor: لما وصف هؤلاء المؤمنين بين أنهم من هم في القيامة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf says maymana and mashʾama mean the right and left sides, or good fortune and ill fortune: people fortunate or ill-omened for themselves.
rows.anchor: الميمنة والمشأمة ، اليمين والشمال ، أو اليمين والشؤم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inbaʿatha is the intransitive counterpart of baʿatha: one sends someone on a task, and he then sets out; here it is the she-camel killer’s arising.
rows.anchor: انبعث مطاوع بعث يقال : بعثت فلانا على الأمر فانبعث له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes the most wretched a specific man, Qudār ibn Sālif, proverbial for ill omen and, by the Prophet’s judgment, the worst of the earlier people.
rows.anchor: أنه شخص معين واسمه قدار بن سالف ويضرب به المثل يقال : أشأم من قدار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the subject as a group, expressed in the singular because the superlative form is invariant across number and gender when annexed; the following plural clause supports this.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكونوا جماعة ، وإنما جاء على لفظ الوحدان لتسويتك في أفعل التفضيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says God owns all of both worlds; human guidance benefits or harms humans, while coercing them would undo moral testing, so God instead guides by explanation, promise, and warning. Al-Razi says this suits Muʿtazilites.
rows.anchor: ( الأول ) : أن لنا كل ما في الدنيا والآخرة فليس يضرنا ترككم الاهتداء بهدانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says God owns both abodes and gives them as He wills, so people should seek happiness in both from Him; al-Razi says this fits his own theology.
rows.anchor: أن لنا ملك الدارين نعطي ما نشاء من نشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse encompasses all ways the Prophet’s renown was raised: prophethood, fame in heaven and earth, his name on the Throne, paired mention in testimony and earlier scriptures, and being the final prophet.
rows.anchor: من النبوة ، وشهرته في الأرض والسموات ، اسمه مكتوب على العرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His name is raised in sermons, the call to prayer, letters, and their openings and endings; Qurʾanic commands repeatedly pair obedience to God with obedience to His Messenger.
rows.anchor: وأنه يذكر في الخطب والأذان ومفاتيح الرسائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made people love mentioning the Prophet and promised affection for believers; the world is filled with followers who praise him, invoke blessings, and preserve his Sunnah.
rows.anchor: وأيضا جعله في القلوب بحيث يستطيبون ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the Prophet’s obedience equivalent to His own and his pledge equivalent to a pledge to God, as the cited verses state.
rows.anchor: جعلت طاعتك طاعتي وبيعتك بيعتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even rulers follow the Prophet; reciters preserve his words, exegetes explain the Qurʾān, preachers convey his counsel, and scholars and rulers seek his service and intercession.
rows.anchor: فالقراء يحفظون ألفاظ منشورك ، والمفسرون يفسرون معاني فرقانك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His honor remains until the Resurrection, as people greet him, touch the soil of his resting place, and hope for his intercession.
rows.anchor: ويرجون شفاعتك ، فشرفك باق إلى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭūr is the mountain on which God spoke to Moses.
rows.anchor: المراد من الطور الجبل الذي كلم الله تعالى موسى عليه السلام عليه

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: Grammarians prefer Sīnīn or Sīnā as a place name for the mountain’s location, or as a name to which the mountain is annexed.
rows.anchor: والأولى عند النحويين أن يكون سينين وسينا اسمين للمكان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿIkrima, says ṭūr means mountain and Sīnīn means beautiful in Abyssinian.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس في رواية عكرمة : ( الطور ) الجبل ( وسينين ) الحسن بلغة الحبشة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses Sīnīn as blessed.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : { سينين } المبارك

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says it is a wooded mountain.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي : هو الجبل المشجر ذو الشجر

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says any mountain bearing fruit trees is called Sīnīn or Sīnā in Nabataean.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : كل جبل فيه شجر مثمر فهو سينين وسينا بلغة النبط

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī prefers Sīnīn as the place name for the mountain; the place was called Sīnīn or Sīnā for its beauty or blessing, and the term cannot be an adjective because it is annexed to ṭūr.
rows.anchor: الأولى أن يكون سينين اسما للمكان الذي به الجبل ، ثم لذلك سمي سينين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The secure town is Mecca; amīn means safe.
rows.anchor: فالمراد مكة والأمين : الآمن

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf derives amīn from trustworthiness: the town protects whoever enters it as a trustworthy guardian protects what is entrusted.
rows.anchor: من أمن الرجل أمانة فهو أمين وأمانته أن يحفظ من دخله

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Alternatively, amīn is a passive adjective from “secure”: the town is protected from harm, like the expression “a secure sanctuary.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون فعيلا بمعنى مفعول من أمنه لأنه مأمون الغوائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of Mecca’s safety is that God protected it from the elephant army.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى حفظه عن الفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that it protects those seeking refuge: even a person liable to death and animals are safe there.
rows.anchor: أنها تحفظ لك جميع الأشياء فمباح الدم عند الالتجاء إليها آمن

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar said he kissed the Black Stone only because he saw the Prophet kiss it, since a stone itself cannot harm or benefit.
rows.anchor: ما روى أن عمر كان يقبل الحجر ، ويقول : إنك حجر لا تضر ولا تنفع

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī answered that it does benefit: God placed Adam’s covenant on a white parchment in the Stone, which had a tongue, lips, and eyes and bears witness to all who come faithfully until Judgment; ʿUmar praised ʿAlī’s wisdom.
rows.anchor: إما أنه يضر وينفع إن الله تعالى لما أخذ على ذرية آدم الميثاق

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Abū Jahl threatened to trample the Prophet’s neck if he saw him praying, but when he did, he recoiled, saying a fiery trench and terrible barrier lay between them.
rows.anchor: أنه قال : هل يعفر محمد وجهه بين أظهركم ؟ قالوا : نعم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says Umayya ibn Khalaf used to prevent Salmān from praying.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أن أمية بن خلف كان ينهى سلمان عن الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse appears to concern the previously mentioned person, hence reports that it was revealed about Abū Jahl; a specific occasion can still have general application, though what follows points to a particular man.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الآية أن المراد في هذه الآية هو الإنسان المتقدم ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Have you seen?” addresses the Prophet in astonishment: he had prayed for Islam to be strengthened through Abū Jahl or ʿUmar, yet Abū Jahl forbids prayer.
rows.anchor: اللهم أعز الإسلام إما بأبي جهل بن هشام أو بعمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jahl was called Abū al-Ḥakam, so it is astonishing to call him wise while he stops worship of God and bows to idols.
rows.anchor: أنه كان يلقب بأبي الحكم ، فكأنه تعالى يقول : كيف يليق به هذا اللقب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fool commands others as though he deserves obedience although he is neither creator nor lord, yet forbids obedience to the true Lord and Creator.
rows.anchor: ذلك الأحمق يأمر وينهى ، ويعتقد أنه يجب على الغير طاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite “a servant” signals complete devotion; an account has a learned Jew ask ʿAlī about the Prophet’s character, and ʿAlī argues that it exceeds description just as the world does, citing scripture.
rows.anchor: أن التنكير في عبدا يدل على كونه كاملا في العبودية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite form also heightens blame by describing the forbidding as the man’s regular habit toward anyone he sees.
rows.anchor: أن هذا أبلغ في الذم لأن المعنى أن هذا دأبه وعادته فينهى كل من يرى

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī saw people praying before the Eid prayer and did not stop them because he feared falling under the verse’s warning against forbidding a worshipper.
rows.anchor: روي عن علي عليه السلام أنه رأى في المصلى أقواما يصلون قبل صلاة العيد

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa adopted this restraint: when Abū Yūsuf asked whether a worshipper should say “God forgive me” after bowing, he prescribed the regular praise and prostration without explicitly forbidding it.
rows.anchor: وأخذ أبو حنيفة منه هذا الأدب الجميل حيث قال له أبو يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also rebukes Abū Jahl for thinking that if Muḥammad did not prostrate, no one else would: countless nearby angels continually pray and glorify God.
rows.anchor: أيظن أبو جهل أنه لو لم يسجد محمد لي لا أجد ساجدا غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite servant magnifies the Prophet: although grammatically indefinite, he is uniquely identifiable, as in Qurʾanic references to God’s servant.
rows.anchor: أنه تفخيم لشأن النبي عليه السلام يقول : إنه مع التنكير معرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse threatens resurrection and full recompense: God knows everything and neglects nothing, so every person will receive complete requital; it warns sinners and encourages the obedient.
rows.anchor: المقصود من الآية التهديد بالحشر والنشر ، والمعنى أنه تعالى عالم بجميع المعلومات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although revealed about Abū Jahl, anyone who prevents obedience to God shares his threat; restrictions in a usurped house or disliked prayer times target sin, as do a master’s or husband’s limits on voluntary worship to preserve welfare with God’s permission.
rows.anchor: كل من نهى من طاعة الله فهو شريك أبي جهل في هذا الوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the books as verses written in the scriptures.
rows.anchor: المراد من الكتب الآيات المكتوبة في الصحف

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: Ṣāḥib al-Naẓm says kutub can mean rulings, as in “God decreed,” and the hadith phrase “by God’s Book” means His ruling; the phrase can thus mean sound rulings.
rows.anchor: الكتب قد يكون بمعنى الحكم : { كتب الله لأغلبن } ومنه حديث العسيف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says qayyima means straight and without crookedness, distinguishing truth from falsehood, as when a proof stands or becomes clear.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : مستقيمة لا عوج فيها تبين الحق من الباطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view understands qayyima as independently standing and conclusive in proof, from the phrase for carrying through an affair properly.
rows.anchor: أن تكون القيمة بمعنى القائمة أي هي قائمة مستقلة بالحجة والدلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the Prophet was unlettered, reciting what is written in scriptures still counts as reciting their contents; a book attributed to Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says he read without writing, perhaps as a miracle.
rows.anchor: إذا تلا مثلا المسطور في تلك الصحف كان تاليا ما فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bi is attached to tuḥaddithu: the earth recounts its news because of its Lord’s revelation to it.
rows.anchor: بتحدث ، ومعناه تحدث أخبارها بسبب إيحاء ربك لها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says “awḥā lahā” means “inspired to it”; al-ʿAjjāj’s line “awḥā lahā al-qarār fa-staqarrat” supports this usage.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : { أوحى لها } أي أوحى إليها وأنشد العجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “for it” means God did this for the earth’s sake, enabling it to exact vengeance on sinners.
rows.anchor: أي فعلنا ذلك لأجلها حتى تتوسل الأرض بذلك إلى التشفي من العصاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mithqāl dharra means the weight of a tiny particle; al-Kalbī says a mote is the smallest ant, and Ibn ʿAbbās says it is each speck of soil stuck to a palm after touching earth. God shows every deed, small or large.
rows.anchor: أي زنة ذرة قال الكلبي : الذرة أصغر النمل

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim reads yarahu with a raised yāʾ; the other readers use fatḥa and some read it in the jussive.
rows.anchor: في رواية عن عاصم : { يره } برفع الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse raises a problem: unbelievers’ good deeds are nullified, while believers’ sins are forgiven, so how can every atom of good or evil be requited?
rows.anchor: حسنات الكافر محبطة بكفره وسيئات المؤمن مغفورة

rows.speaker: أحمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Aḥmad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī says an unbeliever sees the reward of good deeds in worldly life but receives nothing in the Hereafter; Ibn ʿAbbās also reports this, supported by a saying to Abū Bakr about worldly trials and stored reward.
rows.anchor: قال أحمد بن كعب القرظي : { فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة } من خير وهو كافر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God shows every believer and unbeliever all their good and bad deeds; believers are forgiven sins and rewarded for good, whereas unbelievers’ good is rejected and their evil punished.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : ليس من مؤمن ولا كافر عمل خيرا أو شرا إلا أراه الله إياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another answer says the unbeliever’s good is counted as an offset against the punishment due for disbelief, preserving the verse’s general scope.
rows.anchor: أن حسنات الكافر وإن كانت محبطة بكفره ولكن الموازنة معتبرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another answer restricts the general statement: the fortunate see even an atom of good, and the wretched see even an atom of evil.
rows.anchor: المراد فمن يعمل من السعداء مثقال ذرة خيرا يره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked where generosity lies, al-Razi answers that a tiny sin still shows disregard and a tiny obedience still glorifies God, so the generous Lord notices both; the real criterion is sincere intention rather than quantity.
rows.anchor: هذا هو الكرم ، لأن المعصية وإن قلت ففيها استخفاف ، والكريم لا يحتمله

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb warns against belittling any kindness: one person entered Paradise by lending a needle for God’s cause, and a woman by contributing a grain to build Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: روي عن كعب : لا تحقروا شيئا من المعروف

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: When a beggar came as ʿĀʾisha served grapes, she sent him one grape; after others laughed, she cited the verse to teach that tiny acts count. A report says she once gave away 180,000 dirhams in a day and later had only bread and oil for supper.
rows.anchor: وعن عائشة : «كانت بين يديها عنب فقدمته إلى نسوة بحضرتها

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says the verse concerned two men: one dismissed tiny donations, the other minor sins; it encourages small good that may grow and warns small sins may grow into major ones.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : نزلت هذه الآية في رجلين كان أحدهما يأتيه السائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet urged protection from the Fire even with half a date, or a kind word if one has nothing else.
rows.anchor: فمن لم يجد فبكلمة طيبة

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says wasaṭa al-nahr means to reach its middle; wasaṭahā and tawassaṭahā have the same sense.
rows.anchor: قال الليث : وسطت النهر والمفازة أسطها وسطا وسطة ، أي صرت في وسطها

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: One view takes “by it” as the enemy, inferred from the charging horses, and “a gathering” as the enemy host; on the camel reading it means the group at Minā.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : أي بالعدو ، وذلك أن العاديات تدل على العدو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view makes the pronoun refer to the dust: the horses penetrate the host through the dust.
rows.anchor: أن الضمير عائد إلى النقع أي : { وسطن } بالنقع الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view means the chargers penetrated a crowd of enemies while shrouded in dust.
rows.anchor: المراد أن العاديات وسطن ملبسا بالنقع جمعا من جموع الأعداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading doubles the ṭāʾ to make the verb causative; the added bāʾ emphasizes their penetrating the crowd.
rows.anchor: قرئ : { فوسطن } بالتشديد للتعدية ، والباء مزيدة للتوكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the Qurʾān’s brief description of horses is better than the many elaborations people give; the Prophet said goodness is tied to horses and their backs and bellies are treasure.
rows.anchor: وهذا القدر الذي ذكره الله أحسن ، وقال عليه الصلاة والسلام : «الخيل معقود بنواصيها الخير »

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāriʿa derives from striking forcefully and became a name for a great calamity; the word also appears in expressions for blows, a mallet, Qurʾanic passages, knocking, and sword clashes.
rows.anchor: القرع الضرب بشدة واعتماد ، ثم سميت الحادثة العظيمة من حوادث الدهر قارعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes agree that al-Qāriʿa is a name for Resurrection, but differ over the reason.
rows.anchor: واتفقوا على أن القارعة اسم من أسماء القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says the name refers to the blast that terrifies and kills: the first blast removes minds, the second kills all except Isrāfīl, then God revives him and a third blast raises the dead; a report assigns each dead person a trumpet aperture.
rows.anchor: ( أحدها ) : أن سبب ذلك هو الصيحة التي تموت منها الخلائق ، لأن في الصيحة الأولى تذهب العقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the upper and lower celestial bodies collide violently as the world is destroyed, hence the name.
rows.anchor: أن الأجرام العلوية والسفلية يصطكان اصطكاكا شديدا عند تخريب العالم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the calamity strikes people with terrors: the heavens split, sun and moon are folded, stars scatter, mountains crumble, and earth is rolled up and changed.
rows.anchor: أن القارعة هي التي تقرع الناس بالأهوال والإفزاع

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Another view says the Calamity strikes God’s enemies with punishment, disgrace, and humiliation; a verifier prefers it to al-Kalbī’s view because a verse says the faithful are safe from terror that day.
rows.anchor: ( ورابعها ) : أنها تقرع أعداء الله بالعذاب والخزي والنكال ،   وهو قول مقاتل ،   قال بعض المحققين وهذا أولى من قول الكلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled “the Calamity, what is the Calamity?” may be a warning; warnings can use either nominative or accusative, as in “the lion, the lion!”
rows.anchor: أنه تحذير وقد جاء التحذير بالرفع والنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, an omitted clause means “the Calamity will come,” as anticipated by the later phrase about graves being turned out.
rows.anchor: وفيه إضمار أي ستأتيكم القارعة على ما أخبرت عنه

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Another parse makes al-Qāriʿa the subject and “what is the Calamity?” its predicate; Qutrub treats “what lets you know the Calamity?” as the predicate.
rows.anchor: رفع بالابتداء وخبره : { ما القارعة } وعلى قول قطرب الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “what lets you know?” seems to imply ignorance and add no information, it gives new knowledge: this Calamity surpasses ordinary calamities in horror and severity.
rows.anchor: قد حصل لنا بهذا الخبر علم زائد ، لأنا كنا نظن أنها قارعة كسائر القوارع
